cards.f: Blunt — Key Features?
cards.b: Most common cause of serious chest injury. Causes: MVCs, falls, direct blows, crush injuries. Internal injuries may be initially occult and declare themselves later.

cards.f: Penetrating — Key Features?
cards.b: Stab or gunshot wounds. Severity depends on weapon/projectile size, force/velocity, distance, trajectory, and number of injuries. May directly injure the heart → shock/arrest. Bleeding and respiratory compromise are usually more immediately apparent, and unstable patients most often require exploration.

cards.f: Iatrogenic — Key Features?
cards.b: E.g. subclavian central-line insertion → injury to the subclavian artery, lung, or diaphragm → massive hemothorax/pneumothorax. Uncommon but preventable.

cards.f: Stable after an MVA, then mild left chest pain with hyper-resonance
cards.b: traumatic pneumothorax (not primary — there is trauma; not tension — he is stable)

cards.f: The sign that best separates tension pneumothorax from cardiac tamponade
cards.b: breath sounds (absent in tension; both have hypotension and raised JVP)

cards.f: Trauma patient whose NG tube and stomach bubble are seen in the left chest
cards.b: diaphragmatic rupture

cards.f: Immediately life-threatening found on primary survey — Examples?
cards.b: Treated immediately — e.g. airway obstruction, which can rapidly kill the patient.

cards.f: Potentially lethal may emerge on secondary survey — Examples?
cards.b: Traumatic aortic injury/rupture · myocardial contusion · tracheobronchial injury · diaphragmatic rupture · esophageal injury (isolated traumatic esophageal injury is very rare). Associated spinal/vertebral or vascular injuries may coexist.

cards.f: Rule out on the primary survey
cards.b: open pneumothorax (not lung contusion, aortic disruption or diaphragm rupture — those are secondary-survey injuries)

cards.f: Should be dealt with in the primary survey
cards.b: massive haemothorax (aortic and oesophageal injuries are secondary-survey)

cards.f: 80-year-old with 2 rib fractures after an MVA
cards.b: admit and start pain control (elderly = high risk of pneumonia)

cards.f: Rib Level — list them
cards.b: Lower ribs (8–12) · 1st–2nd ribs

cards.f: Significance — list them
cards.b: Suspect associated abdominal/retroperitoneal solid-organ injury — liver, spleen, kidney — despite the diaphragm's protective position. · Fracture = marker of high-energy trauma, since these ribs are short, thick, and protected by the clavicle/shoulder girdle/muscles. Actively search for associated aortic, bronchial, and mediastinal/great- vessel injuries.

cards.f: Not an indication for a chest tube
cards.b: pneumoperitoneum (chylothorax, pneumothorax and haemothorax are)

cards.f: Paradoxical chest-wall segment after a car accident
cards.b: initial management: pain control and oxygen (not a chest tube, thoracotomy or fixation first)

cards.f: True about flail chest
cards.b: paradoxical breathing movement (it needs ≥ 3 ribs in ≥ 2 places, not 5; patients are symptomatic; thoracotomy is rarely needed)

cards.f: Open penetrating left chest wound, laboured breathing, BP 100/70
cards.b: chest tube thoracostomy

cards.f: Open chest wound
cards.b: 3-sided dressing

cards.f: Gunshot with a sucking chest wound, BP 70/30
cards.b: keyed initial step three-sided dressing

cards.f: Upper GI / esophageal — Mechanism?
cards.b: Iatrogenic esophageal perforation after endoscopy/dilatation (especially a diseased esophagus, e.g. achalasia or esophageal cancer); duodenal perforation during ERCP/sphincterotomy (duodenum is vulnerable due to its thin wall); Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophageal rupture).

cards.f: Stab wound to the right chest, BP 80/40, GCS 15
cards.b: chest tube insertion first (haemothorax — drain and measure)

cards.f: MVA, hypotensive, reduced air entry on the right, ABG with hypoxia and respiratory acidosis
cards.b: needle decompression (don't wait for an X-ray, don't intubate first)

cards.f: Site — Detail?
cards.b: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line

cards.f: Technique — Detail?
cards.b: Insert the needle above the rib to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle running below it. Landmark via the Angle of Louis → 2nd costal cartilage.

cards.f: Needle gauge — Detail?
cards.b: Large-bore, approximately 12–14G (14–16G also discussed) — MCQ/OSCE

cards.f: Needle length — Detail?
cards.b: Approximately 5–7.5 cm; a longer catheter may be required depending on chest-wall thickness — MCQ/OSCE

cards.f: Confirmation — Detail?
cards.b: Audible/obvious gush of air on entering the pleural cavity. Remove the metal needle, leaving the plastic catheter in place temporarily.

cards.f: First-line treatment
cards.b: needle decompression, 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, then a chest tube

cards.f: Ideal chest-tube site
cards.b: 5th intercostal space (4th space above the 5th rib), mid-axillary line

cards.f: Landmark that finds the site quickly
cards.b: level of the nipple (≈ 4th–5th ICS)

cards.f: When inserting a chest tube
cards.b: full aseptic technique

cards.f: Sepsis patient 2 hours after a subclavian central line: tachycardia, falling BP and SpO₂
cards.b: tension pneumothorax (iatrogenic)

cards.f: Typical tension picture (unstable, resonant, absent breath sounds, trachea shifted away) → tension pneumothorax ; after an MVA with rib fracture, tracheal deviation and ↓ breath sounds → tension pneumothorax ; motorbike crash, SpO₂ 85%, hypertympanic left chest, BP 80/40
cards.b: tension pneumothorax

cards.f: Side matters: trachea deviated to the LEFT + absent breath sounds/hyper-resonance on the RIGHT
cards.b: needle decompression on the RIGHT 2nd ICS MCL

cards.f: Transfusion of 2 L through a central line — the complication keyed
cards.b: tension pneumothorax (from line insertion)

cards.f: During management of tension pneumothorax, the irrelevant step
cards.b: confirming the chest tube with CT

cards.f: Blunt chest injury with hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad)
cards.b: pericardiocentesis

cards.f: MVA haemothorax, 1800 mL immediately
cards.b: urgent thoracotomy in the OR (an ED thoracotomy is for the arrested patient)

cards.f: Massive initial drainage (~1.5 L) — Action?
cards.b: Indicates surgical bleeding → urgent surgical thoracotomy / operative exploration.

cards.f: Lower initial output (e.g. 500–600 mL), patient stable — Action?
cards.b: Continue resuscitation and monitor tube output very closely.

cards.f: Ongoing bleeding >200–250 mL/hour for 3 consecutive hours — Action?
cards.b: = surgical bleed → OR / thoracotomy — ★ high-yield MCQ

cards.f: Stab wound on the right side of the chest
cards.b: initial step insert a chest tube

cards.f: Gunshot haemothorax, chest tube drains 1600 mL
cards.b: emergent thoracotomy

cards.f: Minor fall, stable, mild SOB, mild pneumothorax
cards.b: observation with supplemental oxygen

cards.f: Pulseless on arrival after a penetrating (stab) wound of the anterior chest, lost the pulse in the ER / pulse 5 minutes ago
cards.b: emergency (resuscitative) thoracotomy

cards.f: Penetrating chest wound with tamponade on eFAST
cards.b: keyed emergency thoracotomy (surgical repair; pericardiocentesis only temporizes)

cards.f: Intubated RTA patient, hard to bag, reduced air entry on the LEFT, trachea to the RIGHT
cards.b: needle decompression on the LEFT 2nd ICS

cards.b: needle chest decompression first

cards.b: chest tube
